nameStory: These magnificent whales earned their name because they were considered the "right" whale to hunt by early whalers. Their slow swimming speed, tendency to float when killed due to thick blubber, and habit of feeding near the surface made them tragically ideal targets for commercial whaling.
description: The North Atlantic right whale is one of the ocean's giants, reaching lengths of up to 55 feet and weighing as much as 70 tons. These massive marine mammals have distinctive dark gray to black skin with white patches called callosities on their heads, and lack the dorsal fin found on many other whales. They're baleen whales, meaning they filter tiny organisms from seawater through comb-like plates instead of having teeth. Sadly, they're among the world's most endangered whales, with only about 356 individuals remaining.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Enormous whale up to 55 feet long with a massive, stocky body and broad back that lacks a dorsal fin - just a smooth, dark curve breaking the surface

idTips.label: Head Features
idTips.description: Large head makes up about one-quarter of body length, with distinctive white or yellowish crusty growths called callosities that create unique patterns like fingerprints

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen skimming slowly at the surface with mouth agape, creating a distinctive V-shaped wake as they filter feed on tiny copepods and other plankton

idTips.label: Blow Pattern
idTips.description: Spout creates a distinctive V-shaped or heart-shaped spray up to 15 feet high due to two separate blowholes

idTips.label: Tail Flukes
idTips.description: Broad, dark tail flukes with smooth trailing edges and a deep notch in the center, often lifted high when diving

habitat: Found in coastal and offshore waters throughout New England, particularly in areas rich with copepods and other small zooplankton. They prefer continental shelf waters and are often seen in Cape Cod Bay, the Great South Channel, and off the coasts of Maine and Massachusetts where cold, nutrient-rich waters support abundant prey.

seasonality.spring: Begin arriving in New England waters as early as March, with peak numbers in Cape Cod Bay and Massachusetts waters for feeding on dense copepod blooms.
seasonality.summer: Concentrate in feeding areas from Cape Cod to the Bay of Fundy, often visible from shore during calm weather as they surface-feed in groups.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding in northern waters through October, building energy reserves before beginning southern migration to warmer calving grounds.
seasonality.winter: Most individuals migrate south to waters off Georgia and Florida for calving, though some may remain in Gulf of Maine if food is abundant.

funFact: Each right whale's head has a unique pattern of white, crusty growths called callosities that scientists use like fingerprints to identify individuals - these aren't barnacles but thickened skin patches that attract whale lice, giving them their white color!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with humpback whales, but right whales lack the humpback's prominent dorsal fin and long white flippers. Remember: "right whales have the right to be finless" - their smooth backs are the giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they were the "right" whale to hunt, this tragic history nearly drove them to extinction. Today, seeing one is extraordinarily rare and special - every sighting should be reported to marine mammal authorities as these encounters help scientists track this critically endangered population.
compareHints: As the only right whale species in New England waters, they're most similar to bowhead whales from Arctic regions, but bowheads have white chins and live in ice-covered waters. Right whales are distinguished from other large whales by their lack of dorsal fin, distinctive head callosities, and V-shaped blow pattern.
